newsitem.title: USA: World Bank says rural poor key to food, environment.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says rural poor key to food, environment.

text.p: Lifting millions of rural people around the world out of poverty is a key to ensuring a secure food supply and protecting the environment, officials of the World Bank said on Monday.

"We are concerned that there is total inadequate interest in rural poverty around the world," Andrew Steer, director of the bank's Environment Department, said at a briefing before the bank's annual conference on the environment this week.

The conference in Washington will focus on ways to improve living conditions in rural areas, which contain about 75 percent of the world's poor, and how that can help improve conditions in urban areas, restore the environment and fight poverty.

"It is not that the rural poor should be helped before the urban poor. The problems of both must be addressed, but the rural poor must not be forgotten in the global rush to modernisation," Ismail Serageldin, the bank's vice president for Environmentally Sustainable Development, said in a statement.
"A thriving rural economy will generate benefits far beyond the boundaries of any local area," he said.

"From the beginning of the industrial age, down to the amazing advances of the East Asian countries of the 1980s, a strong rural economy has been a necessary pre-condition for strong national economic growth."

More than 800 million people go hungry every day and more than 500 million children do not get enough food to fully develop physically and mentally, and most of those live in rural areas, the bank said.
"There is a sort of seduction going on as world food prices have tended to be fairly low, that therefore things are under control with regard to food," Steer said.
"Even when food supplies are fairly ample" the desperately poor in food-producing areas go hungry, he said.
Effective rural development is the best means to fight hunger, increase food production and protect the environment, the bank said.

Food supplies must double by 2025 to meet population growth, meaning far more will have to be produced from the same or a smaller share of land, the bank said. That raises a potential for more hunger and environmental devastation.

"If agriculture is not intensified, in an environmentaly appropriate fashion, then the sheer expansion of the population and its requirement will lead to the destruction of the world's forests from slash-and-burn farming of poor, small holders who barely feed their families," Serageldin said.
